task: This is a synthetic exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes as the fixed record: select, organize and phrase the story without inventing additional reported events, scenes, quotations or reporting activity. Write a headline and a reported feature of roughly 450–650 words in AP style for general newspaper readers about the workshop that repairs public benches for the city of Marrowbank. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 18, 2026.

facts.text: The fictional Marrowbank parks workshop repairs public benches removed from parks, streets and transport waiting areas.
Carpenter Eren Voss begins each job by matching the bench's identification tag to its location and maintenance record.
The supplied scene shows a bench with sound cast-metal ends and several worn wooden slats laid out on the workshop floor.
The crew can replace damaged slats while retaining usable structural parts when the condition assessment supports that approach.
Not every bench can be repaired, and the workshop does not claim that keeping an old frame is always cheaper than replacement.
Voss said, "The tag tells us where it lives. That matters when somebody is waiting for that particular bench to come back."
A removal can leave a gap on a walking route even when several other benches remain elsewhere in the park.
Resident Rella Norn uses one bench on the route between a bus stop and the neighborhood shops as a regular resting place.
Norn said, "I know which bit of the walk comes before it and which bit comes after. Another bench across the grass is not on that walk."
The parks office prioritizes repairs using condition, route need and available parts, rather than simply the order in which a bench was donated.
Under Marrowbank's supplied memorial-bench agreement, plaques are recorded and retained when appropriate, but donors do not receive permanent control over the city's maintenance decisions.
Staff contact the recorded plaque contact when a major change affects an existing memorial bench, using the city's supplied process.
The workshop keeps stocks of common slat sizes, while unusual older designs can require specially prepared replacement pieces.
A newly cut replacement is not installed solely because it matches the color; staff also check its dimensions and suitability for the bench.
The packet gives no universal lifespan for a repaired bench or measured citywide saving from reuse.
The crew records a return-to-service date so the parks office can distinguish work completed in the workshop from a bench reinstalled at its site.
Transport and installation are scheduled with other parks work, so a finished bench may wait briefly before returning outside.
The workshop's wall holds templates for several retired bench designs that still have examples in public use.
Residents can report a damaged or missing bench through the parks service without knowing its inventory number.
The parks office has begun including a location sketch with removal notices after receiving questions about whether benches had been permanently taken away.
The account concerns the repair service, not an announced reduction in the city's total number of public seats.
No private medical history or diagnosis is supplied for the resident who describes using the resting place.

forbidden_additions: Repair always cheaper, a guaranteed lifespan or a citywide seat reduction.
A medical diagnosis for the resident or permanent donor control.
A repaired bench described as already reinstalled without that status.
preserve: The bench as a particular place on a route as well as a repairable object.
The practical sequence from removal and assessment through reinstallation.
Exact quotation wording and attribution when quotations are used.
